# Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta (MN 27 (PTS MN i 175))

**ID:** MN 27 (PTS MN i 175)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint
**PTS:** MN i 175
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta* (MN 27) is the twenty-seventh discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Catalog; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Addressed to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi following a report by the wanderer Vacchāyana, the sutta cautions against drawing hasty conclusions regarding a spiritual teacher's attainments based on outward marks alone [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Peoples 2013]. Just as a wise elephant tracker does not definitively conclude that an elephant is an immense bull merely from sighting large footprints or high scratch marks, one cannot fully know the Buddha or the truth of his teaching until direct realization is achieved [Anālayo 2017; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In the Buddha's formulation, preliminary attainments—such as the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*)—are merely marks or footprints of the Tathāgata; the "elephant" itself is seen only when one attains full awakening and the destruction of the taints [Anālayo 2017; Shulman 2014].

The text embeds this parable within a classic middle-length formulation of the gradual training (*anupubbikathā*), progressing through hearing the Dhamma, renunciation, moral restraint (*sīla*), sense restraint (*indriyasaṃvara*), mindfulness (*sati-sampajañña*), abandoning the hindrances, the four *jhāna*s, and the three higher knowledges (*tevijjā*) [Bodhi 2005; Shonin et al. 2015]. Bodhi contrasts this middle-length schema (sharing three higher knowledges, as also found in MN 51) with the longer paradigm in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), which elaborates eight higher knowledges [Bodhi 2005]. Historically, the sutta holds a celebrated position in Sri Lankan and Southeast Asian chronicle traditions: according to the *Mahāvaṃsa* and the *Jinakālamālī*, it was the first sermon preached by the elder Mahinda upon arriving in Sri Lanka, precipitating the conversion of King Devānaṃpiyatissa and his court [Adikaram 1946; Veidlinger 2007]. Rare Sinhala translations (*sannaya*) of the text survive in Sri Lankan monastic manuscript collections [Berkwitz 2006].
